passages.happening:
“Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven with the key to the Abyss, holding in his hand a great chain” (verse 1).

“He seized the dragon, that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years” (verse 2). “And he threw him into the Abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him, so that he could not deceive the nations until the thousand years were complete. After that, he must be released for a brief period of time” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 19 dealt with the beast and the false prophet. Now the last and oldest enemy, the dragon of chapter 12, meets his end. He is named with his full titles: ‘that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan’. ‘Ancient serpent’ reaches back to the garden of Genesis 3.

Notice who binds him. Not Christ himself, but a single unnamed angel with a key and a chain. The key of the Abyss was given to a fallen star in 9:1 to let the locusts out. Now it locks the Abyss's chief prisoner in. The risen Christ holds ‘the keys of Death and of Hades’ (1:18). Every key in this book is finally in God's hands.

What is stopped is stated exactly: ‘so that he could not deceive the nations’. Deceiving has been his work from the garden onward, and in 12:9 he was called ‘the deceiver of the whole world’. And even his release is God's decision: ‘he must be released’. The word ‘must’ is the word Revelation uses for what God's plan requires. Nothing in the passage gives the dragon a move of his own.

Jesus once said that no one can plunder a strong man's house without first tying up the strong man, and he said it about his own casting out of demons. The Greek verb for ‘bound’ here is the same verb. Many readers connect the two sayings. Others expect a fuller binding still to come. The note on verses 4 to 6 sets out the views.

Jewish writings before Revelation already pictured rebel angels bound and shut away until the judgment. 2 Peter and Jude reflect the same picture.
passages.ot:
Isaiah saw the powers of heaven and earth imprisoned before their final punishment: “In that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below. They will be gathered together like prisoners in a pit. They will be confined to a dungeon and punished after many days” (Isaiah 24:21-22). Many commentators see that pattern, prison first and punishment later, behind this chapter.

And the serpent is the one in the garden, to whom God said, “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (Genesis 3:15).
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the deceiver's power is limited by God, and released only when God allows. Ask which deceptions about God you have found hardest to see through. And ask how Jesus' saying about the strong man changes the way you see his work.

passages.happening:
“Then I saw the thrones, and those seated on them had been given authority to judge. And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image, and had not received its mark on their foreheads or hands. And they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years” (verse 4).

“The rest of the dead did not come back to life until the thousand years were complete. This is the first resurrection” (verse 5).

Verse 6 calls those who share in the first resurrection holy, and says: “The second death has no power over them, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and will reign with Him for a thousand years.”
passages.hearers:
For the first hearers, this vision answered what they feared most. Beheading with a sword or axe was a Roman way of putting people to death, and by tradition the apostle Paul died that way. Those who had refused the beast's worship had lost their lives or their living. In chapter 13 the beast ‘was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them’. Here the verdict is reversed. The court of Rome did not have the last word.

The thrones recall Daniel's vision, where thrones were set and judgment was given in favour of the saints. The souls recall the souls under the altar in 6:9, who cried ‘How long?’. Now they reign.

The phrase ‘a thousand years’ comes six times in these verses, which shows how much weight it carries. The millennium, from the Latin for a thousand years, is named only here in the Bible.

The key word is ‘came to life’. In Greek it is one word, ezēsan, and Revelation uses the same form of Christ's resurrection in 2:8. Whether it means a bodily resurrection here is the centre of the debate. Some argue that if the same word means one kind of life in verse 4 and another in verse 5, the passage cannot be read consistently. Others answer that the passage itself pairs a first resurrection with a second death, so the first of each pair need not be the same kind of event as the second.

Those who share in the first resurrection will be ‘priests of God and of Christ’. That fulfils the promise of 1:6 and 5:10, and the calling given to Israel at Sinai. The hope held out to them is not only survival but a calling: to serve and to reign.

‘The second death’ has no power over them. The phrase comes four times in Revelation (2:11; 20:6, 14; 21:8), always for final exclusion from God's life.
passages.ot:
The thrones and the judgment are Daniel's: “As I continued to watch, thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat” (Daniel 7:9), “until the Ancient of Days arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High, and the time came for them to possess the kingdom” (Daniel 7:22).

And the priestly calling is Sinai's: “And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6).
passages.hard:
What is the thousand years, and when is it?

It is the only place in the Bible that speaks of a thousand-year reign. It is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith; it has never divided the church's creeds. Here are the four views as the book page sets them out, each as its holders would put it. These notes do not choose.

Amillennialists hold that the thousand years is a picture of the present age between Christ's two comings. Christ reigns now from heaven; Satan is bound so that the gospel reaches the nations (Matthew 12:29); the faithful dead live and reign with Christ. Chapter 20 does not follow chapter 19 in time. The return of Christ is one event, followed at once by the resurrection of all, the judgment and the new creation.

Postmillennialists hold that Christ will return after a long age in which the gospel, through ordinary preaching and the work of the Spirit, brings the nations broadly under his rule (Matthew 13:31-33). They say this is not confidence in human nature but in the power of God. Many Puritans, Jonathan Edwards and B. B. Warfield held it.

Historic premillennialists hold that Christ will return before a thousand-year reign on the earth, and that the church will pass through the final time of trouble. They read this chapter in the order it gives: the faithful come to life and reign, and the rest of the dead do not come to life until the thousand years are over. This was the hope of Papias, Justin and Irenaeus; George Eldon Ladd gave it its modern form.

Dispensational premillennialists hold that God's promises to the nation of Israel still stand and will be kept to the letter. Christ will first come for his church in a rapture (1 Thessalonians 4:17), which most place before a seven-year time of trouble drawn from Daniel 9; then he will return openly with his saints and reign from Jerusalem for a thousand years, before a final rebellion, the last judgment and the new creation. John Nelson Darby shaped the system and C. I. Scofield spread it.

All these views agree on what the creeds confess: Christ ‘shall come again, with glory, to judge both the quick and the dead’, the dead will be raised, and God will make all things new. Faithful Christians hold each view, and they are brothers and sisters. Revelation's own interest is less in the order of events than in worship, endurance and hope.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the people the beast killed are the ones who reign. Ask how you hold your own view of the thousand years, with conviction and with humility. And ask how you treat Christians who read this chapter differently from you.

passages.t: Gog and Magog, and the devil's end
passages.happening:
“When the thousand years are complete, Satan will be released from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth—Gog and Magog—to assemble them for battle. Their number is like the sand of the seashore” (verses 7-8).

“And they marched across the broad expanse of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. But fire came down from heaven and consumed them” (verse 9).

“And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, into which the beast and the false prophet had already been thrown. There they will be tormented day and night forever and ever” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
When he is released, the dragon goes straight back to his old work: ‘to deceive the nations’. Whatever the thousand years are, the verses show something sobering. After a long time without the devil's deceiving, the nations still follow him when he comes. Human rebellion is not cured by a better setting. The heart itself must be made new.

‘Gog and Magog’ come from Ezekiel, where Gog of the land of Magog, a northern king, leads a vast army against God's restored people and is destroyed by God. In Revelation they are no longer one king and one land. They are ‘the nations in the four corners of the earth’, humanity as a whole gathered in rebellion. These notes tie Gog and Magog to no nation, people or state, then or now.

The nations surround ‘the camp of the saints and the beloved city’. ‘Camp’ is the word used for Israel's camp in the wilderness: God's people are pictured as still on the march toward their inheritance. And then, again, there is no battle. ‘Fire came down from heaven and consumed them.’ The saints do nothing. God acts, as Ezekiel promised.

This battle looks very like the one in 19:17-21, and both draw on Ezekiel 39. That likeness is central to the debate over the thousand years. Some read the two as one battle told twice, which supports reading chapter 20 as a new view of the same history. Others answer that this battle comes after the thousand years, so it cannot be the battle of chapter 19. These notes do not choose.

The devil is thrown into the lake of fire, where the beast and the false prophet already are. The enemy who first appeared in chapter 12 is finished.
passages.ot:
Gog and Magog are Ezekiel's: “Son of man, set your face against Gog of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal” (Ezekiel 38:2).

The fire from heaven is the judgment Ezekiel foretold: “I will pour out torrents of rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur on him and on his troops and on the many nations with him” (Ezekiel 38:22), and “I will send fire on Magog” (Ezekiel 39:6).
passages.hard:
What is the lake of fire, and does verse 10 teach endless torment?

Christians who share the same creeds read this differently. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Is hell forever, or does it end?’, and the doctrine study on hell set out three views, each held by people who take the warning seriously. These notes do not choose.

The traditional view, held by most of the church through most of its history, holds that the lost will exist for ever under God's just judgment, consciously and without end. It points to this verse's ‘day and night forever and ever’, to 14:11, and to Jesus' words, “And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46).

Conditional immortality holds that the finally impenitent are not kept alive for ever in torment but at last perish. Its holders note that the torment in this verse is said of the devil, the beast and the false prophet, figures that stand for powers rather than individual people, and that verse 14 calls the lake ‘the second death’. They point to Jesus' warning about the one who can “destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matthew 10:28).

A smaller number hope that God's love will finally restore every creature. The church has generally not affirmed it, and many who hold it grant that it goes beyond the church's historic teaching. The New Testament's warnings are severe and real, and every view must reckon with them.

What the church confesses together is that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, that judgment is real and just, and that evil does not have the last word.
passages.asks: Ask why the nations, given a long time free of the deceiver, still follow him, and what that says about the human heart. Ask what it means to you that God ends the last rebellion without his people lifting a hand. And ask how you hold the warning of this verse: with dread, with indifference, or with sober trust in the judge.

passages.happening:
“Then I saw a great white throne and the One seated on it. Earth and heaven fled from His presence, and no place was found for them” (verse 11).

“And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And there were open books, and one of them was the Book of Life. And the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books” (verse 12).

“The sea gave up its dead, and Death and Hades gave up their dead, and each one was judged according to his deeds” (verse 13).

“Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death—the lake of fire” (verse 14). “And if anyone was found whose name was not written in the Book of Life, he was thrown into the lake of fire” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The throne is ‘great’, for majesty, and ‘white’, for purity, the white of the risen Christ in 1:14. The one seated on it is not named here. Elsewhere Revelation seats God on the throne, and later speaks of ‘the throne of God and of the Lamb’ (22:1). Jesus said that the Father has given all judgment to the Son. So the church has read this throne as God's throne, shared with the Lamb. The judge is the one who died for sinners.

Earth and heaven flee from his presence. The old creation gives way before the judge, and the way is cleared for the new heaven and new earth of chapter 21.

‘The dead, great and small’: everyone. No rank exempts anyone, and no one is too small to matter. ‘The sea gave up its dead.’ In the ancient world, to be lost at sea without a grave was counted a special misfortune. No one is beyond God's reach. The dead are raised, all of them, to stand before God. The creeds confess the same: the resurrection of the dead and the judgment of the living and the dead.

Then two kinds of book. ‘Books’ of deeds: the dead are judged ‘according to their deeds’, and no one is judged on anything else. And ‘another book’, the Book of Life, which 21:27 calls the Lamb's. Deeds are real evidence of a life. But the decisive question is whether a name is written in the Lamb's book. Judgment by deeds and rescue by grace stand side by side, as Paul holds them together in Romans.

Then Death and Hades, which have held the dead since the beginning, are themselves thrown into the lake of fire. Death is not only defeated. It is ended. Paul wrote, ‘The last enemy to be destroyed is death’ (1 Corinthians 15:26). Here that promise is carried out.
passages.ot:
The open books are Daniel's: “The court was convened, and the books were opened” (Daniel 7:10). The book of names is Daniel's too: “everyone whose name is found written in the book—will be delivered” (Daniel 12:1).

And the raising of the dead to judgment is Daniel's hope: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2).

God's own heart in judgment is spoken through Ezekiel: “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).
passages.hard:
Should this scene make me afraid? And what of people I love?

The church confesses this judgment. The Nicene Creed says Christ ‘shall come again, with glory, to judge both the quick and the dead’. How final judgment works, and what the lake of fire is, Christians hold in more than one way; the note on verses 7 to 10 sets out the views, and these notes do not choose. These notes say nothing about the eternal state of any particular person. That belongs to God alone.

The picture is not given to frighten God's people. In 13:8 the Book of Life belongs to ‘the Lamb who was slain’, and the names in it were written to steady the persecuted. The one on the throne takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. And the judge is the Jesus who died for sinners.

If you are grieving someone who died without clear faith, these verses may hurt. This passage does not tell us what passed between that person and God at the end. It does tell us who the judge is: the Jesus who died and rose again.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that everyone, great and small, stands before the same throne. Ask how judgment by deeds and the Lamb's Book of Life fit together in your own hope. And ask what it changes to know that death itself will be thrown away.
